name: Sauna

lead: A sauna is a room heated to roughly 70-105 C with low humidity, where you sit and sweat. People in appearance communities use it to look less puffy in the face, recover between training sessions and sleep better, and some say it raises growth hormone.

Heat causes sweating, wider blood vessels and a raised heart rate, a load similar to light exercise. The recovery and relaxation that follow are what users tie to a fresher face and better gains. Published research is mostly about heart and circulation health: a Finnish cohort linked frequent sauna bathing with lower cardiovascular and all-cause mortality, and small trials report improved vascular function. No studies have looked at facial appearance, and a purported study of brow-ridge bone growth that circulates on forums does not appear in the literature.

paras: People use traditional, electric, steam or infrared saunas, often after a workout or in the evening, in sessions of a few rounds with cooling breaks in between. It is commonly paired with hydration, sleep routines and training schedules. Effects on puffiness and relaxation are usually felt the same day, while the cardiovascular research concerns regular use over years.

Alcohol, dehydration and certain heart conditions such as unstable angina or severe aortic stenosis raise risk, and pregnancy calls for limits on core temperature. Rapid sweat-based weight loss, as practised in combat sports, has documented physiological effects. People with heart or blood pressure conditions are generally advised to check with a clinician first.

angle.text: Heat exposure and sweating relax you and help recovery, which users link to a less puffy face and better training gains, and some to higher growth hormone. Finnish cohorts have studied sauna for heart health; the facial and bone claims have not been studied.

lead: A sauna is a small room heated to high temperatures, typically 70-105 C with low humidity, where people sit to sweat, often with bursts of steam made by pouring water on hot stones. [1][2] The practice is most associated with Finland, whose sauna culture UNESCO listed as intangible cultural heritage in 2020. [1] Variants include smoke, electric, steam and infrared saunas. [1]

In looksmaxxing and wider wellness communities, sauna use is discussed for reducing water-retention puffiness, post-training recovery, sleep, and claimed hormonal effects. [3][4] Forum users also circulate a purported study claiming large increases in brow-ridge bone mass; no such study appears in the published literature.

Published research centres on cardiovascular outcomes. A Finnish prospective cohort found that more frequent sauna bathing was associated with lower rates of sudden cardiac death, fatal cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality. [5] Small trials of repeated heat exposure report improved vascular function. [6][7][8] No clinical studies have examined sauna use for facial appearance.

paras: Traditional Finnish saunas are typically heated to about 75-100 C, sometimes higher, and a defining feature is löyly, the steam released when water meets hot stones. [1][2] Smoke saunas lack a chimney and are heated for hours before use, while electric stoves, the most common modern type, warm a room in roughly 15-30 minutes. [1] Steam baths such as the hammam run cooler but near full humidity. [1] Infrared saunas, which heat the body more directly at lower air temperatures, are also sold for home use. [1]

Early forms were pits dug into slopes and used as winter shelters, and Finnish smoke saunas developed over many centuries. [1][2] Electric sauna stoves were introduced in 1938 by Metos in Vaasa, and Finland promoted the sauna at the 1936 Berlin Olympics. [1] Related traditions include the Russian banya, the hammam and Native American sweat lodges. [2] Estonian Võromaa smoke sauna tradition was UNESCO-listed in 2014 and the Finnish tradition in 2020. [1]

The most cited observational study is a prospective Finnish cohort (Kuopio) published in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2015, which reported lower risk of sudden cardiac death, fatal coronary and cardiovascular disease, and all-cause mortality among men with more frequent sauna sessions and longer durations. [5] Observational associations cannot establish causation.

Interventional studies are smaller. Repeated sauna or thermal therapy was reported to improve vascular endothelial function in patients with coronary risk factors and in chronic heart failure, and a single thermal vasodilation session produced acute hemodynamic improvement in heart failure. [7][8][9] An eight-week study of repeated hot water immersion in sedentary young adults reported improved endothelial function, arterial stiffness and blood pressure compared with thermoneutral immersion; this tested water immersion rather than a sauna. [6] A medical review of sauna bathing summarised benefits and risks. [10]

A randomized trial of combined spa and exercise therapy reported benefit in ankylosing spondylitis. [11] No published human trials were found that test sauna use for facial puffiness, brow-ridge bone, or growth hormone as an appearance intervention.

Reviews note that alcohol, dehydration and narcotics increase the risk of sudden death in saunas, that unstable angina and severe aortic stenosis are contraindications, and that people with severe obesity, high blood pressure or diabetes are advised shorter sessions. [1][10] Pregnancy guidance is to keep core temperature at or below about 39 C. [1] The 2010 World Sauna Championships were halted after two competitors collapsed, one of whom died. [1]
A review of weight loss in combat sports describes heat and sweat-based fluid loss as a method athletes use to make weight and discusses its physiological and performance effects. [12]

Members of looksmax.org discuss sauna use as a debloating aid, a post-gym routine, and as part of heat-and-cold contrast routines. [13][14][15] Threads also debate whether heat raises growth hormone, with one popular post asking whether a post-gym session is worthwhile regardless. [4]
